title: D-Wave’s Dual-rail Qubits Detect 90% Of Errors, FirstQFM Confirms
source_used: FirstQFM company release (read), Quantum Zeitgeist rewrite (read)
key_facts: FirstQFM, a Stockholm company that builds AI foundation models for quantum computing, says it is one of four organisations in D-Wave's gate-model beta program.
The others are BBVA, Florida Atlantic University and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre.
The program gives early access to a simulator of D-Wave's dual-rail qubit design ahead of its planned gate-model quantum systems.
D-Wave says the dual-rail design is built to detect about 90% of errors, which reduces the physical qubits and decoding work needed for fault tolerance (D-Wave's own claim).
A Nature publication recently showed a fast, high-fidelity two-qubit gate that keeps the error-detection property.
FirstQFM plans to use the simulator to test how detected errors and real-time control can improve quantum calculations.
D-Wave CEO Alan Baratz called error correction 'a defining challenge in the race to commercially useful gate-model quantum computing'.
quote_evidence: D-Wave’s dual-rail qubit architecture is designed to identify approximately 90% of errors by encoding quantum information across two modes, allowing for the localization of errors as erasures rather than complete data loss.
FirstQFM, BBVA, Florida Atlantic University, and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre will gain early access to a simulator of this technology as part of D-Wave’s new gate-model beta program.
The program aims to prepare participants for future dual-rail gate-model hardware and explore error-aware programming approaches.
why_it_matters_hint: Early users can practise error-aware quantum programming before D-Wave's hardware exists; the 90% figure is D-Wave's own claim.
event_date: D-Wave launched the beta program on 1 Oct 2026 (press-release copies listed on Google News dated 1 Oct); our 7 Oct 2026 edition carried it; FirstQFM's own statement is dated by Quantum Zeitgeist 7 and 10 Oct 2026
notes: Repeat of a story already in our 7 Oct 2026 edition (D-Wave beta program, entry C15-11 of that day, which named FirstQFM and the other three participants); the only addition is FirstQFM's own statement of how it will use the simulator. Quantum Zeitgeist's piece is a rewrite of FirstQFM's release, so the release (firstqfm.com) was read too and is the source. All claims are company claims; the Nature paper was not opened.
